lesson.title: Why More Trials, Not Balancing Out, Gets You Closer to the Truth
lesson.summary: The law of large numbers says the observed relative frequency of an outcome drifts closer to its true probability as the number of independent trials grows, but it says nothing about individual outcomes evening out or being due.
lesson.body:
The law of large numbers states that for a random phenomenon with true probability p, if you repeat the process independently a great many times, the proportion of trials, not the count, that produce the outcome tends to get closer and closer to p as the number of trials grows without bound. This is precisely why probability was defined earlier as a long run proportion in the first place, and it is why simulation works at all: running more trials makes the simulated proportion a more trustworthy estimate of the true probability.

The most important and most misunderstood part of this law is what it does not say. It does not say that outcomes must balance out, and it does not mean that a run of one result makes the opposite result more likely soon afterward. If a fair coin lands heads on each of its first 5 flips, the probability the 6th flip is tails is still exactly 0.5, not higher, because each flip is independent and the coin has no memory of what came before. Believing the coin somehow owes you extra tails to even things out is the gambler's fallacy, and it is simply wrong.

What actually happens as the number of trials grows is that any fixed early imbalance gets swamped, as a proportion, by the sheer volume of new trials, even though the raw gap in counts does not have to shrink and can even grow. Here is a worked, purely hypothetical illustration. Suppose in the first 10 flips of a fair coin you happen to get 7 heads. That is a relative frequency of 7 divided by 10, or 0.70, noticeably far from the true probability of 0.5, and 2 more heads than the 5 you would expect on average. Now suppose you keep flipping until you have done 1000 flips in total, and by then you have recorded 508 heads out of 1000, a perfectly plausible result for a fair coin. That relative frequency is 508 divided by 1000, or 0.508, much closer to 0.5 than 0.70 was.

Look closely at the counts behind those two proportions. The excess of heads over the expected number actually grew, from 2 extra heads after 10 flips, 7 versus an expected 5, to 8 extra heads after 1000 flips, 508 versus an expected 500. The count of "extra" heads did not shrink at all, it grew. Yet the proportion moved from 0.70 down to 0.508, landing much nearer the true probability of 0.5. That is the law of large numbers in action: convergence happens in the proportion, driven by the growing number of trials in the denominator, not because the coin does anything to correct or cancel out its earlier counts.
